utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IT-01-47T, the Prosecutor against Mr. Hadzihasanovic and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the parties please introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning Your Honours. For General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic and Stephane Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Representing Mr. Kubura, Mr. Ibrisimovic, Rodney Dixon, and our legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All the parties present, the accused and everybody here are greeted by the Trial Chamber. We must continue with our work today with the hearing as planned, two witnesses. I looked at the planning this morning. One half hour was planned for each of the witnesses. We will see if we can finish with the two witnesses today or perhaps the second witness will have to be continued tomorrow, on Wednesday. If there is nothing else to say, we can perhaps usher in the witness. Would the usher please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I will see if the equipment is working, and if what I'm saying is properly interpreted. Tell me that you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. -- you were called as witness by General Kubura; that is, his Defence team. Before reading the solemn oath, will you please give your name, date, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Elvir Musija born on the 1st of August, 1971 in Akat [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me which town or which village because it was not properly recorded? Could you spell, perhaps, the name of your village or town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] T-a-k-a-n-j.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Kakanj, K-a-k-a-n-j.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am employed with a construction company as a driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, 1993, did you have an occupation? Did you work? If you were a military person, in which way were you involved in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I was with the Territorial Defence of Kakanj municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Municipal Staff. I was with the Territorial Defence until September 1993. After that, I transferred to the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, did you testify before, before this International Tribunal or before any other national court about the events in 1992 and 1993 or is it the first time you're appearing before the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you now read the solemn declaration given you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before giving the floor to counsel, I will give you some information about the way in which this hearing will be conducted. You have already met the counsel of General Kubura who have certainly given you some explanation about the way these proceedings work. First of all, you will be answering questions asked to you by Defence counsel of General Kubura. After that, the counsel of General Hadzihasanovic, who are seated behind the counsel of General Kubura, will be able to ask you questions also if they wish so. After that, the Prosecution, which is on your right side, will also ask you questions which is called here cross-examination. They will be asking you questions, therefore, that are directly linked to the questions that were asked by Defence counsel. After that, counsel of General Kubura will have a chance to ask you additional questions, a redirect in response to the questioning to the Prosecutor. The three Judges before you normally can ask you questions at any moment; however, we prefer to hear out everybody first to finish with the examination of both parties and if we ask any questions, it will be either to clarify the answers that you had given to the previous questions or we will be asking you questions, because in the interests of justice, we have to have some additional information from a person who was on the spot at the relevant time. I will draw your attention to another two things that are important. First of all, you have declared that you will speak the truth and the whole truth, and as you know, lying in a court of law is a violation that is subject to very serious penalty. And secondly, if we ask you a question and you decide that the question itself and the answer you might give might turn against you and might incriminate you, you can answer, "I absolutely do not wish to answer this question." This is a situation we have never encountered here before but in any case -- in this case, we have the right to ask you to answer the question nevertheless by granting you immunity. We have no documents accompanying your testimony which is why your oral testimony is all the more important. You will be answering questions and this will be put on record which is here called the transcript. That will be the record of your testimony. Therefore, please try to be precise in the answers you are giving. If you do not understand a question, please ask the person asking the question to clarify it. Sometimes questions can be complicated and you may not understand them. Even the Judges sometimes do not understand the questions that are asked. That is why it is absolutely necessary for the witness to perfectly understand the question that he is asked to answer. And generally speaking, if you have any difficulty of whatever kind or manner, you have the right to draw our attention to it. If you need a break, you can ask for it. In any case, we are obliged to stop every 90 minutes for a break but if at any moment you wish to address the Judges, you have that right to. I will now give the floor to Mr. Dixon who is completely prepared by now and who will commence the direct examination. Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Musija. Sir, you said in response to a question by the President of the Trial Chamber that you were a member of the 7th Brigade from September 1993. Can you give the exact date and in what position were you a member of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I believe the exact date is the 1st of September, 1993. In the establishment post of courier or messenger escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Why were you appointed into this particular position?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, the need arose for that because Mr. Kubura became commander in August, sometime in August 1993, the need arose for such an establishment post so I was transferred to the 7th Muslim Brigade to that particular establishment post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Were you working directly for Mr. Kubura in this position?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: When you say "escort," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: That means that in the event we were going out into the field, I would make the preparations for that. When he would go out into the field, I would take care of accommodation. And I did other work related to the organisation of his departure, journey, and return.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you offer protection to him while he was in the field?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes. During the way there and back and the stay in the field, I also performed tasks related to security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And when you say that you were a courier, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: As a courier, I would summon officers to meetings, make announcements, take the mail from Mr. Kubura to his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you have an office, and where were you based?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I did not quite understand. Do you mean where I was staying during that time in the barracks or in the field?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Let's start with the barracks. Where were you stationed in barracks? And then after that, if you could explain where you would be stationed when you went into the field, generally?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: While we were in the barracks, I would spend my time in the anteroom before Mr. Kubura's office and on the ground, I had accommodation in the building right next to the building where Mr. Kubura was so that he was able -- in fact, I was able to be available to him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the first time that you met Mr. Kubura during the war?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: The first time I saw Mr. Kubura was in December 1992 when I got my transfer orders from the Territorial Defence to the 3rd Mountain Battalion, that is, from the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Would you please clarify, you mentioned it was the 3rd mountain -- in the transcript it says "battalion." Is that right? Is it not the 3rd Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: It was a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And what brigade was that battalion part of?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: It was the 333rd Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: In December 1992, what position did you hold in that 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I occupied the establishment post of soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Kubura's position?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: He was battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: As a soldier in his battalion, did you have much contact with Mr. Kubura during that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, I didn't have much contact with him because most of my time was spent in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You stayed in that battalion until the 1st of September, 1993, you've said.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: In December 1992, did you have any contacts or joint operations with the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: When you came to the 7th Brigade at the beginning of September 1992 [sic] to work for Mr. Kubura, what position did he hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: He occupied the post of brigade commander whereas my job within the perimeter of the barracks was to announce the arrival of superior officers, accommodation for them, all the organisational work within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: The transcript needs to be corrected. The question that was asked was when the witness arrived at the beginning of September 1993 to work for Mr. Kubura. From September 1993 until the end of November 1993, can you recall how many times you went out into the field on military operations with Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I think it was on three different occasions, three different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Was one of those areas Vares?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: That was in the beginning of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Can you assist the Trial Chamber with what occurred at the commencement of that operation and how the events unfolded with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. operation?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: We organised movement from Zenica Bilmiste village towards the village of Strijezevo which is close to Vares. We travelled in a small sedan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you there, when you say we travelled, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I mean Mr. Kubura, myself, and his driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And on what date was that that you drove to Vares?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, I don't know the date. It was the beginning of November. I know it was a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: If you could assist with explaining the journey that you took and what events unfolded, please?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: So we were travelling from Zenica towards Strijezevo village. Those were army roads, not paved roads such as a macadam road, for instance. When we arrived at Strijezevo, we found accommodation. The commander was billeted in a private house, and I was billeted in a house next door, also privately owned. I will note that Strijezevo is a Bosniak village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: When you arrived there on that day, do you recall what preparations were made during the course of that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: All I know is that meetings were held with commanding officers, of which I summoned some, but I can't remember their names. In any case, all sorts of meetings were held. I did not have insight into the subject of these meetings so I can't tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the military operation commenced?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: The military operation commenced the next day in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: What was Mr. Kubura doing at this time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: That morning, I received orders that we would be leaving for Vares and I remember from Strijezevo towards Vares, we travelled along a mountain macadam road arriving at Vares Majdan, a place which is a kilometre away from Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: When you say "we were travelling along that mountain road," are you referring to yourself and Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to myself, Mr. Kubura, and the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Where were the units of the 7th Brigade at this time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: As far as I knew at the time, the units were in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: When you arrived at Vares Majdan, as you said, what did Mr. Kubura do at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: When we arrived at Vares Majdan, we reached a military police checkpoint. We stayed there for about one hour. Mr. Kubura had conversations over a mobile radio set and then we returned to the village of Strijezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You mentioned a military police checkpoint, do you know which military police were stationed there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: It was the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you see any other brigades or units at that checkpoint in Vares Majdan?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: In the immediate vicinity of the checkpoint, I saw a couple of members of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I saw a unit from Visoko. I don't know which structure it belonged to. I also noticed that there was a UN personnel carrier in the vicinity of this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you see any UN soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes, they were in position in the vehicle itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You said you returned to Strijezevo, so you did not go into the town of Vares on that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know what was happening in the town?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: When you returned to Strijezevo, can you recall what time of the day that was?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: It was about 11.00 or 12.00, about noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: What did Mr. Kubura do when he got back to Strijezevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Some meetings were held with battalion commanders. I think there was some other officers there but I can't remember very well. I don't know what was at stake. When we returned to Strijezevo, our soldiers told me that Vares had been abandoned, so that it was an abandoned town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "our soldiers," do you mean soldiers from the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Can you assist the Trial Chamber when the units of the 7th Brigade that you mentioned earlier that were advancing on Vares, when they returned from the Vares area to Strijezevo or its surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Shortly after our return, perhaps two or three hours later -- this took place in winter so the night fell very early, and until night fell, I saw that the unit that was located in Strijezevo was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: What happened the following day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: On the following day, in the morning, I received an order from Mr. Kubura to get ready to go to Vares. I was told that some sort of a demonstration had been organised there by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: In the transcript, the word "demonstration" has been referred to. Could you explain for the Trial Chamber what, in fact, had been organized by the civilian authorities in Vares on that following day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: They had organised the takeover of the municipality of Vares. They were taking control of it. So it was a celebration to mark the takeover of Vares by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you then accompany Mr. Kubura to Vares?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I left with him from Strijezevo but, as I wasn't part of the programme for that gathering, I remained at the military police checkpoint in Vares Majdan and he continued to travel to Vares with his driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: How long did Mr. Kubura stay in Vares on at that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, for about two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing during that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: While you were at the checkpoint, could you describe what you witnessed there? What was happening at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Civilian vehicles arrived. Because of the gathering that had been organised, naturally the military police performed their duties, they checked the vehicles and the passengers and drivers in the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: When Mr. Kubura returned after attending these functions in Vares, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: When all this was over, we returned to Strijezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And after that, what was your next move?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I received an order from Mr. Kubura to pack my affairs and I was told that we were returning to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Packing and getting ready took about an hour, and then we set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And do you know what had happened to the units of the 7th Brigade at that time on that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about the unit that was deployed in Strijezevo. That was the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade. By the end of the day, they had returned to the Bilmiste barracks in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned two days that you were in the Vares area. During that time, did you receive or convey any reports to Mr. Kubura about looting in the area?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, I didn't but given the nature of my duties and tasks, I didn't have any access to documents and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you see any troops of the 7th Brigade carrying any items that had been looted or taken from households?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, I saw the troops returning to the barracks in buses, naturally they had their own equipment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I want to move off Vares now and look at the time from the 1st of September that you were working directly for Mr. Kubura. Throughout that entire period, can you assist the Trial Chamber as to whether or not Mr. Kubura ever visited the music school in Zenica in that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did he ever speak to you about the music school or did anyone ever speak to him in your presence about the music school?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, he didn't, and I wasn't even aware of the existence of that music school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know where the music school is situated now?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: In order to get from the 7th Brigade headquarters in Bilmiste to the 3rd Corps headquarters elsewhere in Zenica, can you help us: Is it necessary or do you have to drive past the music school to get there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: That road doesn't go by the music school so you don't have to pass by the music school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you continue working for Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, from September 1993 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Was this always in the 7th Brigade or did you move to another brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: It wasn't always in the 7th Brigade. Sometime in March, I don't know the exact date - in 1994, though - we received an order transferring us to the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And how long were you working for him in the 1st Corps for?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So how many years would that approximately be?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: A year and a half or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: In what position did you work for him?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: As a courier, an escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Having worked closely with Mr. Kubura from the 1st of September, 1993 until the end of the war as you've just explained, could you give your impressions of Mr. Kubura as a military commander both as somebody based in his barracks, but also as somebody commanding in the field?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, I can say that Mr. Kubura is an officer who requested that orders be obeyed, he demanded that the troops conduct themselves in a military manner and he had a saying. He would say that it was necessary to have order and discipline in the army and at the same time, he socialised with the soldiers and officers from his brigade. He helped the soldiers. He tried to keep the level of morale at an adequate level so the soldiers liked him. They grew to like him. I could also add something else. I remember that at the end of December and in January 1993 or between 1993 and 1994, in our military canteen, we had sour cabbage for breakfast, lunch, and dinner with a slice of bread. There was nothing else to accompany the meal so he shared everything with his soldiers. While we were in the field, he would organise, together with the locals, on the whole, women, the preparation of food which he would personally distribute to the soldiers at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few follow-up questions. When you said that he focused on order and discipline, could you explain to the Trial Chamber what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, discipline, it means performing your duties in accordance with orders issued by your superiors. We paid a lot of attention to hygiene, that also comes under the heading of order. The troops were lined up when they were about to go to have their meals and they also had to greet their officers, conduct themselves in a military manner. That's about all I could say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And what was his approach or what were his relations with the soldiers that he commanded?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: He would socialise with the troops. He would put them at ease. Sometimes we would have a laugh, he would tell a joke to help the soldiers forget about the situation they were in, about the fact that they were soldiers, et cetera. Naturally, this was all done in his free time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: What was his approach to the opposition that he was fighting? And also, what was his approach to different groups, different religions in the area where he commanded?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, like all of us, he lived in the state called Yugoslavia and people learned to be cooperative and this is a trait that he retained. He had nothing against the people as such. Naturally, as far as his enemy is concerned, well, war is war. I remember that when he went to visit his family, which was living in Kakanj -- well, there's a road that passes by two buildings, it passes by an Orthodox church and a Catholic church, and he would often say that we were proud of the fact that these two buildings had been left intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: As a final question, could you say in just a few sentences what it was like to be commanded by Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: It was an honour for me. I think that most of the soldiers liked Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. him and many of them wished that he was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Musija. I have no more questions but there might be some more from the Prosecution and from Their Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, we have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then, that proceeded very rapidly. I'll ask the Judges if they have any questions. Well, I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were a courier and escort, General Kubura's security -- he was the brigade commander. Could you tell us why the brigade commander engaged someone who wasn't in the 7th Brigade before September, someone he confided in, or was it quite by chance that you happened to have this role of assisting him?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, in December 1992, we were together in the 3rd Mountain Battalion of the 333rd Brigade where I was engaged as a private. He saw certain qualities in me. He believed that I was courageous and honest so I believe that it is these qualities that he had in mind and since I am from Kakanj, he engaged me because I thought that we would manage to work with each other more easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you were with him until when, exactly?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question, you mean in the 7th Brigade or up until the end of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of war. Until when, exactly, were you with Brigadier Kubura up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date but it was up until the end of the war, up until the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were with him in September 1993, in September, October, November, December, and then the beginning of 1994, did you hear anything about an El Mujahed unit, did you hear about any such a unit?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: As I'm from Kakanj, I wasn't familiar with what was taking place in Zenica naturally. I had heard about that unit but I never had any contact with this unit nor did I ever see those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said that you heard about the unit but what did you hear about this unit?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: You have to believe me if I say that I really don't know. Not much was said about them. I had my own work that I tried to perform as well as I could and these foreigners were of no interest to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said "these foreigners were of no interest to me" because you did hear that these units consisted of foreigners, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, this unit comprised men including some from foreign countries. There were locals too, but since I was from Kakanj, I was not very familiar with Zenica. I didn't know where they were quartered and I had no contact with them either in the barracks or in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the month of September when you were at the side of the brigade commander, you were in the Bilmiste barracks, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, personally, did you have a room within the barracks or were you quartered somewhere outside?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I had a bedroom within the barracks. It was, in fact, a dormitory where soldiers slept. It was very near the office of Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that period, September, October, November, December, did you receive pay? Did you have a salary? Because normally, soldiers receive a salary, pay.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, we didn't get anything. As far as I can remember, during that period, I was in the 7th Brigade, I received a package, a parcel with some staple food. That is the same that I received when I was in other units such as the municipal staff of the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that you had no salary but you received a parcel containing food like compensation. This food parcel, did you receive it every month or it was never planned, it came when it came?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, whenever there was food available, the superior commands would distribute it across units and I received some too. Food was in very short supply at the time. There was very little to go around, great shortages, so that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A soldier like you, a private, if he was brave, if he conducted himself well on the front line, did he receive financial rewards or did he receive some additional benefits in the form of food? Were there any special rewards like that? Did you personally receive any?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You received no award, no reward?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you finish your career as a private or did you eventually get a rank?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: As a private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You have explained that you were in Vares, that you made a journey together with the driver of Mr. Kubura, and Mr. Kubura himself, and you said when you were travelling, the units were in front of you. At the time when you were on your way, who was carrying the radio communication device?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Kubura. It was a hand-held radio, a Motorola GP-300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this hand-held radio, GP-300, during all the time you were with the brigade commander, did he always have this Motorola with him or did he carry it specially on that occasion or was it rather that by definition, the brigade commander always had this radio on him?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: He always had this radio with him, radio that was drawn from supplies, and he needed it to maintain communication with his subordinate commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of your knowledge, since you were close, after all, to the brigade commander, was communication normal and regular or was it hindered, riddled with problems? What can you tell us about communication, of course seen from your level, from what you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, I could not notice much because I had no contact with signalsmen, people handling the communications equipment, so I really can't tell you much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Early this morning, you said that you would sometimes carry mail to superior commanders. Could you tell us under what circumstances the brigade commander would give you something to take to the 3rd Corps, did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Such things would not happen. I would never carry anything directly to the 3rd Corps command, no documents or communications, but what I would receive in the field, communications, was they would always be in a closed envelope so I could not see what it was and what it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the ground, you said you would sometimes receive communications that were in a closed envelope. Where did you take them and to whom?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Kubura would place it directly in my hands and I was to hand it in personally to the addressee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who were the addressees, officers, or who?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Our commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Battalion commanders?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Sometimes it would be a battalion commander if a battalion commander was close by, and if I could easily go see him, then I would carry the mail to him. But sometimes I would carry something for commanding officers in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brigade commanders, do you mean other brigades, commanders of others -- other brigades? Could you tell us which brigades, if you can remember, because this was quite some time ago, years ago. Those were communications that were addressed personally to the commanders of other brigades. Do you have a clear memory of those packages, mail that you gave to --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't say the commanders of other brigades, I meant only the commanders of our battalions and commanding officers within our brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. I also understood you as saying that one of your duties was to provide security to the brigade commander, can you confirm that? Can you confirm that among your other multiple tasks, you were also practically the bodyguard of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: When we would be in the field or when we would be travelling, I played that role, but when we were in the barracks in Bilmiste, there was no need for me to provide security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you assumed your duties, did you know that the brigade commander had sometime previously been the subject of an assassination attempt?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were securing the commander in the field, it was to protect him from who, from the HVO, from the Serbs, who did he need protection from?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I was guarding and protecting him from any activity by hostile forces, enemy forces. And if I may add, we were always in the field where there were troops all around, fighting was going on, so my job was to look after him, to be close by, to protect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm coming back to Vares. You said at one point that when you arrived at Vares Majdan, you encountered a checkpoint manned by the brigade's military police. How many men were there at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Four to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of your knowledge, did the military police of the 7th Brigade play within this brigade an important role? How did you perceive the role of the military police? Could you inform the Trial Chamber of your opinion of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, within the perimeter of the barracks, they guarded the gates to the barracks and they performed regular duties. For instance, if a soldier would fail to come back from leave in time, they would be sent to fetch him. Those were the basic duties of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you know, were the military policemen some soldiers who could be qualified as elite soldiers or could anybody become a military policeman? For instance, could you, if you had wanted to, become a military policeman or were some particular qualities required?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Not necessarily. For instance, if somebody had served in the former Yugoslav Peoples' Army as a military policeman, he had that particular registered military specialty, and he could then become the -- a military policeman in our army because he was familiar with the duties of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About Vares, if I understood you correctly, you arrived there coming from Bilmiste. You were on your way to the Strijezevo village, and the next day, you travelled on to Vares Majdan and then you came back to that village the day after next after which you returned to the barracks in Bilmiste. Can you tell us exactly how many days did you stay out in the field, two days, three days?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: The first day when we came to Vares Majdan, we only stayed for an hour. After that, we returned to Strijezevo village the same day, an hour later, we returned to Strijezevo. And it was only the next day in the morning that we went to Vares Majdan again and on that occasion, I stayed at the checkpoint held by the military police while Mr. Kubura, accompanied by his driver, went to Vares. It was around 3.00 p.m. -- correction, three hours later we returned to Strijezevo and then went on back to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said that the brigade Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander, Mr. Kubura, had gone to Vares town while you personally had stayed at the checkpoint held by the military police. So if he had gone to Vares town, how long after that did he come back?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Three hours later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when he had come back to Vares town, did he tell you anything, did he share with you any impressions or did he tell you anything at all? And why didn't he take you to Vares town with him?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me anything in particular after he had come back from Vares except that this civilian ceremony of handover, takeover of power or government to civilian authorities had taken place. And the reason that I didn't go was that I was a simple soldier, whereas this event had been organized by civilian authorities and I was not included in the programme developed by the protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So who was guarding him then, because you weren't around?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: There was civilian police already available in Vares and they provided security. The protocol section probably assigned civilian police to provide security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for three hours, you were at the checkpoint where you probably talked to those military police.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I didn't talk with them about anything in particular, I just rested. I was looking around to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while he was -- while you were there, were they checking soldiers who were coming back from Vares or were they, perhaps, doing no checking at all? Were there units, troops, coming back from Vares?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: There was some vehicles passing by, civilian vehicles. Some of then went to Vares and came back. Two small cars, for instance, and in their case, the military police checked both the passengers and the vehicles. As for troops, there were no troops that day. At least I didn't see any in Vares Majdan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, to your knowledge during those checks made by the military police, were any soldiers found in possession of property such as money or food that they had taken in Vares or perhaps you didn't hear anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I have already said I didn't see any soldiers passing through that checkpoint. Two to three civilian vehicles passed through carrying civilian passengers and they were subjected to normal checks of both the persons and the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have one follow-up question concerning this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, these two or three civilian vehicles with civilian passengers, you observed the military police checking both those civilian vehicles and the civilian inhabitants of those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what steps the military police took with respect to the civilian passengers, did they ask to see their papers, did they physically search them? What steps did you observe the military police undertaking with respect to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, the check looked like this: First, their papers were checked, personal IDs, driver's licences, documentation for the vehicle. The passengers did not actually get out of the car because they were representatives of civilian authorities who were on their way to attend the ceremony in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about any civilian vehicles or civilian persons coming out of Vares, that is, travelling southbound through Vares Majdan?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: The same routine control check of the boot of the car, documentation on the car, et cetera, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So the civilian persons in the car remained in the car at that point in time or did they get out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: They did not get out. The driver was the only one to get out to open the boot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel of Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have just a few questions to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Commander Kubura had a small radio. Would you please tell me if that was a radio providing an open-type of communication. In other words, not secured communications, the radio could not be used for any confidential secure communication?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Every radio station had its code, code name and code language so whenever such messages need to be transmitted, the code words would be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But my question had a different objective. That communication, whatever it was despite the fact that it was coded could be intercepted by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: I am not a signalsman, I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said that you played the role of messenger for the commander and you transmitted messages to various commanders within the brigade, commanding officers. You said that when you say commanding officer, that could mean battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could that imply also the members of the command of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So every contact you had performing that function was within the limits of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you spoke of communications on the part of the commander through that radio he had, did he use that radio to contact with the commanding officers of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that radio was a means for him to communicate with his subordinate commanders such as battalion commanders and other commanding officers within the 7th Brigade itself?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Only one matter to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned earlier that there was a UN presence at this checkpoint in Vares Majdan. Can you just clarify when you saw the UN there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: We saw the members of the UN troops at the very entrance to Vares Majdan in the vicinity of the checkpoint held by the military police. That was on the day when the operations took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And where were the UN troops in relation to the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: They were to the right of the checkpoint. On the Vares-Majdan-Vares route, there was a checkpoint at a crossroads and to the right, on the road to the right goes from the crossroads, that is where the UN personnel carrier was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Can you remember how close that was to the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: It was about 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And on the day of the operation when you were there at the checkpoint, do you recall what the military police were doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Well, they were checking the soldiers who were returning from Vares and who were passing through. I don't know what their duties were exactly, though. But on the whole, these soldiers who were entering and leaving Vares on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: On the following day when you stated that you saw the civilian vehicles being checked by the military police, was there still a UN presence there at that point?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were there. And that was probably their checkpoint or observation point. I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: They were stationed at the same place, about 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR MUSIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this completes your testimony. On behalf of the Judges, I would like to thank you for having come to testify in The Hague at the request of Brigadier Kubura's Defence counsel. I wish you a safe trip home. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we have our break, I would like to ask the Defence whether the second witness is ready? Can we commence with the examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is ready and I think we can start hearing the witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well in that case we will now adjourn and we will resume at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume and I will ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying into your own language. If so, please tell me that you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for Brigadier Kubura's defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Fuad Kulovic, I was born on the 16th of June 1961 in Kakanj in the municipality of Kakanj in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I operate turbines in the Kakanj thermoelectric power plant at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind and if you were a member of the military, could you tell us which unit you were a member of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I held the same position in the Kakanj power plant and that was the case up until April 1994 when the aggression commenced in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In April 1994, I was mobilised by the Territorial Defence Staff in Kakanj where I remained until the end of 1992. I was then transferred to the mountain battalion which was based at the open-cast mine in Kakanj. I remained there until the end of March 1993 and then I was transferred again to the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade in Kakanj. The position I had was within the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that on line 17 and 18, page 32, it was not 1993, it was 1992. Sir, have you ever testified before a national or international court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I have appeared before a court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. Before I give the floor to Defence counsel who will commence with the examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information to ensure that everything runs smoothly. First, as Brigadier Kubura's Defence has certainly explained to you, you will have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to answer the questions that they will put to you. According to the schedule, Defence counsel will require about one and a half hours to question you about the events that you were a direct witness of or that you heard about. Afterwards, the Prosecution may -- afterwards, General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team may put questions to you and then members of the Prosecution may conduct the cross-examination. As a rule, the Prosecution can take the same amount of time for their cross-examination which means that if it took the Defence an hour and a half to examine you, the Prosecution is allocated the same amount of time. After this stage has been completed, Brigadier Kubura's Defence may ask you additional questions that relate to the questions put to you by the Prosecution. Then, the three Judges who are before you may also ask you questions. Perhaps you are wondering why the Judges will question you. Judges question witnesses because this is provided for in the Rules of Procedure but sometimes it is necessary for the Judges to clarify certain answers or the Judges believe that information is missing, information that needs to be obtained in order to determine the truth. In such a case, the Judges may ask you to express your opinions on certain matters. Once the Judges have finished putting their questions to you, we give the floor to the Defence and the Prosecution so that they can ask you any questions that arise from the Judges' questions. And naturally, Defence counsel is the last to take the floor and ask you questions. I also need to inform you of two other matters. You have taken the solemn declaration. You have said that you will speak the truth. You have just said that this is the first time that you have appeared before the Tribunal. You have said that you will speak the truth and this excludes the possibility of giving false testimony, naturally. False testimony is punishable by this Tribunal and a sentence not exceeding 7 years could be imposed on a witness for giving false testimony. And there is another thing I'd like to point out to you. This is part of the common law procedure, but you have the right to refuse to answer a question if you believe that your answer could be used to prosecute you at a subsequent date if you believe that your answer could incriminate you. In such exceptional circumstances, and so far we have never had such a case, in such exceptional circumstances, the Judges may compel you to answer the question because given that you have come to testify at The Hague, it is your duty to answer questions. If you are, however, you are compelled by the Judges to answer such a question, you are granted immunity; whatever you say cannot be used against you. But as I have already said, such a case has never arisen yet, and we hope that he with will never have to deal with such a case. As the procedure followed here is based on the common law procedures, the procedure is oral. We have no written documents. We know nothing about the testimony that you will be giving. Whatever you say will be appearing on the monitor in front of you. The transcript on the monitor is in English. If you understand English, you can follow the transcript that appears on your monitor. If you don't understand English, you will have to rely on the interpreters who are interpreting what I am saying in French and what the other parties, the Prosecution will be saying in English. Since the procedure is oral, it is very important for you to provide full and extensive answers. Try to be as precise as possible because as I have already said, we have no documents concerning your testimony. So it is your testimony that will establish, that will form the transcript. When I say the transcript, I'm referring to everything that appears on the screen whenever someone takes the floor. If you feel that a question is too confused or you don't understand it, don't hesitate to put it to the party asking you to rephrase it so that you can answer the question as fully and as precisely as possible. It's possible that you might be shown documents in the course of the proceedings, either military documents or documents that you may be familiar with or documents that you should be familiar with, given the position that you held in the past. Perhaps you will be shown documents, perhaps not; we will see. But if such documents are shown to you, the reason for showing them to you will be to ask you for your opinion on the contents of the document. This hearing should be completed by 1.45. We will be having a 20 to 25 minute break given the need to change the tapes and also -- and in order to have a break so that you can have a rest. Answering questions incessantly can be quite tiring. According to the schedule, you will be testifying today and perhaps your testimony will continue tomorrow. This all depends on the time the Defence counsel and the Prosecution will need to examine you. It might be necessary for you to return tomorrow. If you run into any difficulties in the course of the proceedings, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We are here to deal with any problems that may arise. This is the information that I wanted to provide you with in order to ensure that the proceedings run smoothly. I will now give the floor to the Defence for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We believe that we will need an hour and a half for the examination-in-chief of this witness, or that was what we believed we would need. But in fact, we believe that it won't take more than 45 minutes. So apart from some very general questions, we wanted this witness to testify about the events in Kakanj in the middle of May 1993 and about the events in the Sretno Motel so we believe that there will be sufficient time to complete the witness of the hearing of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, you have already answered a number of questions put to you by the Presiding Judge about what you were doing in 1992 and 1993. Perhaps it wasn't quite clear when you said that you were first a member of the Territorial Defence and you said that you became a -- the member of a certain battalion, which battalion was it and which brigade?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: That was the battalion that was part of the 333rd Mountain Brigade which was located in Busovaca municipality and that battalion, I don't know who ordered its formation, was in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: While you were a member, of the Territorial Defence in Kakanj municipality and while you were a member of this battalion of the 333rd Brigade, did you meet Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Kubura in August 1992 and he appeared there from the former JNA, he appeared in the Territorial Defence Staff. That was the first time I saw him. I hadn't known him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are just a few documents that we would like to use. I believe I would like to show these documents to the witness. We have a sufficient number of copies for everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the document dated the 5th of September, 1992. Do you recognise the document? I have already shown it to you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign that -- who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by the then commander of the Territorial Defence, Ibrahim Hukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 1(a) where it says the 1st Battalion, it says Kubura Amir the 1st Battalion commander, what is this order about?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: It says "Amir Kubura," it says he was the deputy commander of the 1st battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just say within which military formation?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this document shows that Mr. Amir Kubura, when he arrived in August 1992, I think that was the date, I can't remember the exact date, but when he arrived, when he appeared, the command of the Territorial Defence appointed him as the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion. As far as I can remember at the time, the commander of that battalion was Huzezner [phoen]. I think that was his name but it's not stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have a look at the second document dated the 1st of December. It's the command of the 3rd Corps -- it's from the command of the 3rd Corps of the armed forces and under item 1(a) have a look at that part of the document. Have a look at 1(a) and could you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can see an order here which was drafted by General Enver Hadzihasanovic and Kubura Amir is being appointed as the commander of a mountain battalion of the 333rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kulovic, until when exactly were you a member of the 333rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date but I'm sure that it was up until the end of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When and in what manner did you arrive in the 7th Muslim Brigade and where did you report to exactly?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I was transferred for the secretariat for national defence. I was transferred to the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade which at the time that I arrived there was based in the Doboj primary school. In fact I was born in Doboj, so I am very familiar with that school. And we were billeted in that primary school in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Were you assigned an establishment post or duties of any kind?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the battalion, there was a vacant post for an intelligence officer so I was offered this post. I had never performed such duties before but we were all amateurs in any case and we went to war, we left the factory and went to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the duties of an intelligence officer. What sort of duties did you have to perform?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was involved in certain operational intelligence about the Serbian aggressor. I was involved in gathering intelligence, to the extent that I was capable of doing that. I had to obtain intelligence about the enemy's movement, the enemy's objectives. I obtained such information from the soldiers who would return from the lines from other brigades from the civilian population and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the headquarters of the battalion were in the primary school, do you know whether the headquarters of the 3rd Battalion were located somewhere else later on?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how all of this took place. I don't know who issued the orders but I know or rather I assume that an order was issued by the municipality of Kakanj. Since the children had to go to school an order was issued to make the school available and we were transferred to the Sretno Motel which assume was available at the time. I don't know the exact date, but we moved out of the school and we moved into the Sretno Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, were you in Kakanj in mid-May 1993 when there was an incident between members of the 7th Brigade military police and members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Kakanj or to be more precise, at the time I was in the motel when the military police, the brigade military police from Zenica came to the Sretno Motel. I had heard that they had come to Kakanj to bring in some members of the 7th Muslim Brigade who had failed to report in time after they had been granted leave, they had failed to report back to their units and I didn't speak to them at the time. I had no contact with them but I heard that they were supposed to bring in members of Papratnica or some other village, a village near the power plant, but they were supposed to bring in these men from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second. Can you remember when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in the afternoon. I can't tell you precisely what time it was but it was certainly in the afternoon. So they left, probably towards the thermal power plant and an hour later, maybe half an hour late - I wasn't paying attention because we didn't know what was going to happen - three military policemen came, three or maybe four, came back to the motel, taken aback, a little frightened, we asked them what happened and they said they had been ambushed. They couldn't tell us exactly where they had been ambushed because they don't know Kakanj and the surrounding area and they said they had been encircled and managed to get out. Three or four of them managed to get out while the others remain encircled and these three didn't know what was going on with their comrades.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So what happened after you received this information?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: There was some troops at the motel, panic seized the troops because these military policemen told us they had been fired at, they didn't know whether their friends had been killed or wounded. All of us were frightened of what might happen next. We didn't know at first what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to do. We were taken aback, taken completely by surprise. Very soon after that, somebody informed us by telephone that this battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade should not go anywhere, should not leave the motel at all because the 309th Brigade was involved and Kakanj was in their zone of responsibility. I went to the command of the 309th Brigade to see if they had any better information about what was going on on the ground. I believe I found there Dzemal Hadzic who was then commander of the 309th Brigade. He was talking on the phone with Nevin Maric, commander of the HVO. And he was asking Mr. Nevin Maric to refrain from doing anything foolish, I believe that's exactly what he said, "foolish," and to let those policemen go. I went out of that office, I found a lot of people had gathered around, many troops and other people. Anyway, the commander of the 309th Brigade left the headquarters and I later found out that he had gone to the thermal power plant for negotiations with the HVO. I believe the French Battalion of the UNPROFOR was at the time stationed at the thermal power plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Were Mr. Catic and the deputy commander involved in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them coming and going from the command but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I meant to ask you, did you see them at the command even though they were not directly involved in the negotiations with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them coming to the command of the 309th Brigade. Anyway, I spent all this time there, both the civilian and military police were there communicating through their radios, the civilians, the troops could use the roads. The civilian and military police were located in some sort of catering establishment near a place called Rampa, owned by a certain Mr. Sikira. Those policemen had been locked up there, whereas one of them was dragged off by the HVO. Where they didn't know, but it was somewhere towards the Sutjeska river. We received information that the UNPROFOR was following the developments; however, some troops came and told us that these policemen who had returned from encirclement gathered some members from around the motel in order to exchange them for the members of the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What time was it then?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: It was already late. It was almost night as far as I can remember. Can I continue? Late that evening, since I was constantly at the headquarters of the command, I know that an APC of the French Battalion of the UNPROFOR hauled in that member who had been kidnapped from the group and the man was completely beaten up, black and blue. They carried him out on a stretcher. He had been beaten on his elbows and knees and I believe men from the 309th Mountain Brigade took him to the hospital, whether to Zenica or to Kakanj, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that all that time you were at the command. Which command?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 309th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive information at some point whether the negotiations had taken place and whether they were successful?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago, but I know that negotiations did take place and the UNPROFOR had that information. Agreement was reached to -- to make an exchange between the HVO and the 7th Muslim Brigade. Anyway, sometime during the night, they were released. I'm just trying to remember ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that happened? Was it late in the evening or ...

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in the evening. I can't tell you the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who brought those people to the Sretno Motel?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I received complete information only the next day. I was very tired that night. I spent the night at home because my home isn't far away from this place, and the next day when I returned to the motel, I was informed that members of the brigade military police had brought in those HVO members and, as I was told, when they saw what had happened to their colleague, they were provoked into creating this accident. I would really call it an accident. They beat up this HVO man; that was their reaction. And I can tell you that what happened at the motel was not staged and was not organized by anybody, it was not planned for us as a unit to create problems with the HVO and to raise the tensions. We had our hands full with our -- with our one enemy, we didn't need anymore. So I would really call it an accident. I wish it hadn't happened, but it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the light of what you just said, do you know if any HVO members had been brought in before what you call "the accident"?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, we had no detention facility at the motel. All the quarters were private. Perhaps somebody was brought in for an interview but I didn't see any of that. This one ugly incident is the only thing that I saw happening at the motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What information did you receive the next day when you arrived at the battalion? Did you learn whether those people were released?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the battalion, there was no one at the motel. The exchange had already taken place. I can't remember when they were released, whether it was in the morning or during the night. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said you had met Mr. Kubura back in August 1992. Was Mr. Kubura in Kakanj that day or maybe the next day?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kubura's post was in Zenica. I am certain that I personally did not see him in Kakanj either the day before or on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, we would like to use one more document of the Prosecution, namely P564. With your leave, we would like to show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm seeing it for the first time or maybe I saw it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Look at item 5. Actually, para 1, it says "relocate to Zagradje village." Do you know whether it is?

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: Zagradje village, I believe, is two or three kilometres away from my home, from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Look at item 5, it says "Inform the commander of the 7th Mountain Brigade 3rd Battalion -- sorry, the commander of the 7th Brigade's 3rd Battalion shall inform the commander of the 309th Brigade and the commander of the Kakanj Municipal Staff." I would like to know whether this Zagradje village is in the Kakanj municipality or some other municipality.

utterances.speaker: FUAD KULOVIC
utterances.text: This document certainly refers to Zagradje village in Kakanj municipality because I have been there and some of our troops were always located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions for this witness and our examination is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness at the moment, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
